design-variables-s1.title: How far does water climb a paper strip?
design-variables-s1.text: A student cut strips of the same filter paper, all 15 cm long, in four widths. She hung each strip so its bottom 1 cm dipped into a beaker of water at room temperature, and after 10 minutes measured how high the wet front had climbed. She tested three strips of each width.

table.caption: Height reached by water after 10 minutes

design-variables-s2.title: Evaporation at three temperatures
design-variables-s2.text: A class put 50.0 g of water into identical open dishes and left them for 24 hours in warming cabinets set to 20, 30 or 40 °C, three dishes per temperature. They weighed each dish at the start and end. The 40 °C cabinet was the only one with a small fan inside to keep its temperature even.

table.caption: Mass of water lost from each dish in 24 hours

items.q: In this investigation, what are the independent and dependent variables?
options: Independent: width of the strip. Dependent: height the water climbed in 10 minutes.
Independent: height the water climbed. Dependent: width of the strip the student cut.
Independent: the type of filter paper. Dependent: the time the strips were left in water.
Independent: the 10-minute time limit. Dependent: the width and the height of each wet strip.

why.correct: The student chose four widths (the factor she changed) and measured the height of the wet front (the response).
options: Correct: she set the width and measured the height.
This reverses them; the height is what she measured, not what she set.
Paper type and time were kept the same for every strip; they are controlled variables.
The time was fixed for all strips, and the width was chosen, not measured.

items.q: Select ALL of the factors that were controlled variables in this investigation.
options: Type of paper
Width of the strip
Time before measuring
Height of the wet front
Mean height for each width

why.correct: Controlled variables are kept the same for every strip: the same filter paper, the same 10 minutes and the same 1 cm dipped in.
options: Controlled: every strip was cut from the same filter paper.
Not controlled: width is the independent variable, the factor deliberately changed.
Controlled: every strip was measured after 10 minutes.
Not controlled: height is the dependent variable, the measured result.
Not controlled: the mean height is calculated from the dependent variable after the run.

items.q: Which conclusion do these data support?
options: Over this range, strip width had no clear effect on how high water climbed in 10 minutes.
Wider strips pulled water higher, because a wider strip has more paper for water to stick to.
Narrower strips pulled water higher, because their mean height at 0.5 cm was the largest value.
The investigation failed, because a well-designed experiment shows a difference between groups.

why.correct: The means (6.1, 6.2, 6.0, 6.1 cm) differ by less than the spread within each width (strips of the same width differ by up to 0.5 cm). There is no trend with width.
options: Correct: the differences between means are smaller than the differences among repeats of the same width.
The means do not rise with width: 4.0 cm strips averaged the same as 0.5 cm strips.
The 0.5 cm mean (6.1 cm) is not the largest, and a 0.1 cm difference is far smaller than the variation among repeats.
A result showing no effect is a real finding when the design is sound; experiments test, they do not have to show a change.

items.q: Water climbs paper because water molecules are attracted to the paper fibers (adhesion) and to each other (cohesion). Which testable question would best follow from these results?
options: Does the type of paper affect how high water climbs in 10 minutes?
Why does water like to climb up paper instead of staying in the beaker?
Is filter paper the most interesting paper for studying water?
Would water climb a strip faster if the strip wanted to get wet?

why.correct: A testable question names one factor to change (paper type) and one result to measure (height in 10 minutes). Different papers have different fibers and spaces between them, so adhesion could differ.
options: Correct: one factor to change, one measurable result.
It asks about water "liking" something, a purpose, and names no measurable result.
"Most interesting" is an opinion; no measurement can answer it.
Paper does not want anything; the question cannot be tested by measurement.

items.q: Which feature of the procedure most weakens the conclusion that temperature alone caused the 40 °C dishes to lose the most water?
options: Only the 40 °C cabinet had a fan, so moving air was a second difference between the groups.
Three dishes per temperature is too few repeats for any comparison of the means to be made.
The dishes were weighed at the start, which could have disturbed the water before the experiment.
Mass of water lost is a dependent variable, so it is not possible to control it during the experiment.

why.correct: Moving air carries water vapor away from the surface and speeds evaporation. Because the fan was only in the 40 °C cabinet, the 40 °C group differed in two ways, so the extra loss cannot be credited to temperature alone. Air movement should have been a controlled variable.
options: Correct: two factors changed together, so their effects cannot be separated.
Three repeats is few, but the 40 °C dishes (6.9-7.5 g) do not overlap the others; the bigger problem is the second difference.
Every dish was weighed the same way, so weighing is the same in every group and cannot explain a difference.
The dependent variable is measured, not controlled, but that is how every experiment works, not a weakness.

items.q: What percentage of its starting 50.0 g of water did a typical 30 °C dish lose in 24 hours (use the mean)? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
Which is the best if-then prediction for this experiment?
options: If the water temperature is higher, then more water will evaporate in 24 hours, because more molecules have enough energy to break their hydrogen bonds and escape.
If water evaporates, then the temperature of the cabinet will rise, because evaporation releases heat into the surrounding air and warms the inside of each cabinet.
If the dishes are identical, then the experiment will be fair, because identical dishes hold the same mass of water.
If more water is lost, then the temperature was higher, because hot water evaporates.

why.correct: An if-then prediction starts with the independent variable (temperature), states the expected change in the dependent variable (mass lost) and gives a reason (more molecules can break free of their hydrogen bonds).
options: Correct: IV in the "if", DV in the "then", reason after "because".
This reverses the variables, and evaporation removes heat from what is left behind rather than releasing it.
This describes a controlled variable, not a prediction about the dependent variable.
This runs backward, from result to cause, and the reason simply repeats the claim.

items.q: The class wants a group that shows how much water an open dish loses with no warming at all. Which addition is the best control group?
options: Three identical dishes of 50.0 g water left at room temperature in a cabinet that is switched off, with no fan
Three dishes of 50.0 g water at 50 °C, to extend the range of temperatures that were tested
One dish of 50.0 g water sealed with a lid in the 40 °C cabinet, to show what happens when no water can escape the dish
Three dishes holding 100.0 g of water at 20 °C, so that more water is available to evaporate

why.correct: A control group gets the baseline condition (no warming) while everything else matches the experimental groups: same dishes, same mass, same cabinet type and the same time.
options: Correct: baseline temperature, everything else identical, with repeats.
A 50 °C group is another experimental group, not a no-warming baseline.
A sealed dish changes a different factor (open versus closed) and is a single dish, so it is not the baseline for open dishes.
Changing the mass of water adds a second difference instead of providing a baseline.

items.q: A student puts ice cubes of equal mass into cups of water at 10, 25 and 40 °C and times how long each cube takes to melt. Which variable is the dependent variable?
options: Time for the ice cube to melt
Starting temperature of the water
Mass of each ice cube
Volume of water in each cup

why.correct: The melting time is the result measured in response to the water temperature the student set.
options: Correct: it is measured, and it responds to the temperature.
The water temperature is set by the student: the independent variable.
The cube mass is kept equal: a controlled variable.
The volume should be kept the same: a controlled variable.

items.q: To test whether salt affects how fast water cools, a student puts plain water in a glass beaker and salt water in a plastic cup, heats both and times the cooling. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The container differs as well as the salt, so a difference in cooling time could come from either one.
The student should measure temperature instead of time, because time is not a dependent variable.
Salt water and plain water are different liquids, so comparing the two in one experiment is not a fair test.
There is no hypothesis, and an experiment run without a written hypothesis produces no usable data.

why.correct: Glass and plastic conduct heat differently. With two factors changed, any difference cannot be traced to salt. The container must be a controlled variable.
options: Correct: only the salt should differ.
Time to cool is a perfectly good dependent variable.
Comparing them is the point: salt is the independent variable.
A hypothesis helps planning, but data from a sound design are usable either way; the real flaw is the second variable.

items.q: Which question is testable in a controlled experiment?
options: Does adding soap change the number of drops of water a coin can hold?
Is water the most important substance for living things on Earth?
Why do water molecules prefer to stay close to each other?
Should students drink more water during exams to stay alert?

why.correct: It names one factor to change (soap) and one result to measure (drops held).
options: Correct: one factor changed, one result measured.
"Most important" is a value judgment, not a measurement.
Molecules do not prefer anything, and the question names no factor to change.
"Should" asks for advice; it is not answered by a measurement.

items.q: Why does a well-designed experiment test each condition several times?
options: Repeats show how much the results vary by chance, so a real difference between groups can be told apart from that variation.
Repeats make each individual measurement more accurate, because the equipment warms up and settles after the first use in a session.
Repeats guarantee that the hypothesis is correct, as long as the repeats give matching results.
Repeats let the investigator choose the result that best fits the prediction and report that one.

why.correct: Single measurements vary. With repeats, you can see the spread within a group and judge whether the difference between groups is bigger than that spread.
options: Correct: repeats reveal chance variation.
Repeats do not change how accurate any one measurement is; they show how much measurements differ.
Matching results support a hypothesis but do not prove it.
Picking the best-fitting result is cherry-picking; every repeat is reported.

items.q: What is the difference between a control group and a controlled variable?
options: A control group is a whole group given the baseline condition; a controlled variable is one factor kept the same in every group.
A control group is the group kept at room temperature; a controlled variable is the factor the investigator deliberately changes between groups.
They are two names for the same thing: anything in the experiment that the investigator does not change.
A controlled variable is the group with no treatment; a control group is the factor kept the same everywhere.

why.correct: One is a group for comparison; the other is a factor held constant across all groups.
options: Correct.
The factor the investigator changes is the independent variable, not a controlled variable.
They are different: one is a group, the other is a factor.
This swaps the two definitions.

items.q: Put the steps of planning a controlled experiment on evaporation in a sensible order.
options: Write a testable question: does temperature affect evaporation?
Choose the independent variable and its values (20, 30 and 40 °C).
Decide how to measure the response at each of those temperatures (mass lost in 24 h).
List the controlled variables (dish, starting mass, air movement, time).
Run several dishes at each temperature and record every value.

why.correct: Question first, then what you change, what you measure, what you hold constant, and finally repeated runs.

items.q: A student predicts: "If the water is warmer, then it will climb filter paper faster, because warm water molecules move faster." She finds warm and cold water climb to the same height in 10 minutes. What do these results show about the prediction?
options: The results do not support the prediction about height at 10 minutes, but speed early in the climb might still differ.
The prediction is proven wrong, so faster-moving molecules can have no effect on how water travels through paper of any kind.
The results support the prediction, because both samples of water climbed the paper strip.
The results tell her nothing, because the student did not use a control group with no water.

why.correct: Data can fail to support a prediction without proving the whole idea wrong. She measured final height at 10 minutes, while the prediction is about speed; the two can differ.
options: Correct: not supported for what was measured, and the mismatch between "faster" and "height at 10 min" is worth noticing.
One result does not prove an idea false for every case, and her measurement did not match the prediction's variable.
Both climbing is expected either way; support needs the predicted difference.
Warm versus cold already gives a comparison; a strip with no water would tell her nothing.
